title: Why the Best People Leave First
author: McGinnis, Kelly
summary: Kelly McGinnis argues that when turnover happens, the departure order is not random -- the best performers leave first, and this pattern is a diagnostic signal that most leaders misread as ordinary attrition. The article identifies four conditions that reliably drive top performers out: work beneath their capability, promotions going to less-qualified people, lacking access to leadership visibility, and cultures where excellence goes unrewarded. McGinnis argues that the exit of a single top performer is recoverable, but several exits in sequence signal a structural problem about the organization's values and systems. The piece provides a framework for leaders to read the departure order, identify the underlying cause, and intervene before the next exit.
points: The departure order is diagnostic: when top performers leave first, it reveals that the organization is systematically undervaluing excellence -- this is a structural signal, not random noise.
Top performers are exquisitely sensitive to the reward structures of an organization: when promotion, recognition, and interesting work go to average performers, the best people notice immediately.
Organizations often misread top-performer exits as personality conflicts or personal decisions: the systemic cause -- a culture that doesn't reward excellence -- goes unaddressed.
Leaders can reverse the pattern by changing one visible thing: publicly rewarding and promoting the best performers sends an unmistakable signal about what the organization values.
Some contexts are genuinely not worth fixing: if the organization's values are misaligned with excellence, the most useful thing a leader can do is be honest about that and support the transition.
quotes: The order of exits is a signal. Most leaders assume it's turnover. It's not.
Your best people have options. They always do. When they leave, it's not because they couldn't find work somewhere else. It's because they couldn't find what they needed here.
The A-players leave. Then the B-players start looking. Then you're left building with what remains, wondering what happened to the team you thought you had.
If you're the one being left, don't waste the signal. The best people are telling you something on their way out. The only question is whether you're able to hear it.
Fixing the system that drove them out matters more than replacing the person who left. Replace without fixing, and you'll lose the replacement too.
